findings.summary: In the migrate-loop `case "$status" in ... esac`, the catch-all `*)` branch that logs a FAILED migration no longer increments `failed` (the original code had `failed=$((failed + 1))` here; the refactor dropped it). Since `failed` is now only ever incremented in the `ensure_org` failure path, a repo that fails to migrate (e.g. Gitea returns 500, or the request times out per the new --max-time bound) is logged to stderr but never counted. The script's final exit gate `[[ "$failed" -eq 0 ]] || exit 1` (line 171) will therefore report success (exit 0) even when individual migrations failed — silently breaking the exit-code contract a cron/alerting consumer relies on. This directly undermines the brief's own goal of letting callers 'reliably branch on status codes ... across the enumeration and migration loops', since the loop no longer acts correctly on a detected failure status.

findings.summary: The brief asks to 'bound how long any single request can run.' This was added to gitea_api (--max-time 1800 / 60) but gh_api has no --max-time (or --connect-timeout) at all. Since gh_api is called in the pagination `while :; do ... done` enumeration loop, a stalled/hanging connection to api.github.com can block the script indefinitely — the exact failure mode the timeout requirement was meant to close, and it applies to one of the two named helpers but not the other.

findings.summary: gitea_api's timeout branch is keyed on 'has a data payload', so the fast org-creation POST (`/api/v1/orgs`) inherits the same 1800s ceiling intended for the slow synchronous-clone migrate POST. Not incorrect, just looser than necessary — a stalled org-creation call could hang up to 30 minutes before the bound kicks in.
